summary: This informational RFC defines concepts and terminology for SIP in a peer-to-peer setting, where the proxy-registrar and routing functions are replaced by a distributed mechanism, such as a distributed hash table. It includes a high-level view of how the parts relate.

plainLanguage.summary: SIP phones normally find each other through a chain of servers. This document describes an alternative: a shared network of peers, each one storing a share of the phonebook and passing messages for the others. The document's purpose is to define the words used to describe that arrangement and to show how the pieces fit together.

questions: how does overlay network routing work
what is a distributed hash table
subtitle: How a SIP phone can find another phone through a shared overlay instead of a central registrar.

tldr.problem: In ordinary SIP, a fixed hierarchy of proxies and registrars maps a user's name to the address where the user can be reached, and that hierarchy is a single point of failure and a fixed cost for every deployment.
tldr.mechanism: P2PSIP replaces the hierarchy with an overlay network whose peers run a distributed hash table. Each peer stores part of the name-to-address mapping and forwards messages for the others.
tldr.outcome: The result is a server-less SIP deployment in which the mapping is spread across the peers, with the document defining the terms used to describe it.

today: RFC 7890 is an Informational document published in June 2016. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it is an overview rather than a specification: the protocol it describes is specified in RFC 6940 and the companion documents.

sections.title: The Problem P2PSIP Sets Out to Solve
sections.content:
One of the fundamental problems of multimedia communication between Internet nodes is the rendezvous problem: discovering the host at which a given user can be reached. In the Session Initiation Protocol, this is expressed as the problem of mapping an Address of Record (AoR) for a user into one or more Contact URIs. The AoR is a name for the user that is independent of the host or hosts where the user can be contacted, while a Contact URI indicates the host where the user can be contacted.

In the common architectures referred to as Conventional SIP or Client/Server SIP, there is a relatively fixed hierarchy of SIP routing proxies and SIP user agents. To deliver a SIP INVITE to the host where the user can be reached, a user agent follows the procedures in RFC 3263 to determine the IP address of a SIP proxy, and then sends the INVITE to that proxy, which delivers it in turn to the hosts where the user can be contacted.

This document describes an alternative solution. The relatively fixed hierarchy of Client/Server SIP is replaced by a peer-to-peer overlay network, in which the mappings of AoRs to Contact URIs are not centralized at proxy and registrar nodes but are distributed amongst the peers in the overlay.

The details of that solution are specified by the RELOAD protocol, which defines a mechanism for distribution using a Distributed Hash Table and specifies the wire protocol, security and authentication mechanisms needed to convey the information. The RELOAD protocol was designed specifically with a distributed SIP registrar in mind. Other applications were considered while it was being designed, and design decisions were made that allow RELOAD to be used elsewhere, but only where those decisions did not add undue complexity to the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: To call someone, a SIP phone has to turn a name into an address. Today it does that by asking a chain of servers. This document asks what happens if the phonebook is spread across a network of peers instead, so that no single server has to hold it all.

sections.title: What an Overlay Provides
sections.content:
A P2PSIP Overlay is a collection of nodes organized in a peer-to-peer fashion for the purpose of enabling real-time communication using SIP. Collectively the nodes provide a distributed mechanism for mapping names to overlay locations, which gives the mapping of Addresses of Record to Contact URIs and so provides the location server function of RFC 3261. An overlay also provides a transport function by which SIP messages can be transported between any two nodes in it.

An overlay consists of one or more nodes called Peers. The nodes collectively run a distributed database algorithm, which allows data to be stored on nodes and retrieved in an efficient manner. The algorithm may also ensure that a copy of a data item is stored on more than one node, so that the loss of a node does not lose the data item to the overlay.

Peers offer both distributed storage and distributed message-routing services. The RELOAD protocol also offers a simple discovery mechanism specific to the TURN protocol used for NAT traversal, and individual peers may offer other services, such as voicemail, or to support applications beyond SIP, in which case they may need to store additional information in the overlay.

An overlay may also include nodes called Clients. Clients are supported in the RELOAD protocol as peers that have not joined the overlay, so they do not route messages or store information; they access the services of the protocol by connecting to a peer that performs operations on their behalf. There is no distinct client protocol: a client connects using the same protocol but never joins the overlay as a peer.

A special peer may also be a member of the overlay and may present the functionality of a SIP registrar, proxy or redirect server to conventional SIP devices, so that existing unmodified SIP clients may connect to the P2PSIP network. Such a device is also sometimes called a client, which is a distinct concept from the Client defined above, because it does not speak the RELOAD protocol.

Network Address Translators are impediments to establishing and maintaining peer-to-peer networks, since they hinder direct communication between nodes. Some peer-to-peer architectures avoid the problem by insisting that all nodes exist in the same address space. RELOAD instead provides capabilities that allow nodes to be located in multiple address spaces interconnected by NATs, to allow RELOAD messages to traverse NATs, and to assist in transmitting application-level messages, such as SIP messages, across NATs.
sections.plainLanguage: The overlay does two jobs. It stores where each user can be reached, and it carries messages between the peers. Peers that have joined the network store data and forward messages for the others; clients use the network without joining it, and ordinary SIP phones can reach it through a peer that behaves like a normal SIP proxy or registrar.

sections.title: The Words the Document Uses
sections.content:
An overlay network is a computer network built on top of another network, where nodes are connected by virtual or logical links, each corresponding to a path, perhaps through many physical links, in the underlying network. A peer-to-peer network is one that relies primarily on the computing power and bandwidth of the participants rather than concentrating them in a relatively low number of servers.

A Peer is a node participating in a P2PSIP overlay that provides storage and transport services to other nodes. Each peer has a unique identifier, known as a Peer-ID, within the overlay, and each peer may be coupled to one or more SIP entities. A Client is a node that participates in the overlay but does not store information or forward messages; it can be thought of as a peer that has not joined the overlay, and it can store and retrieve information from the overlay.

A Resource is anything about which information can be stored in the overlay; both users and services are examples. A Resource-ID is a non-human-friendly value that uniquely identifies a resource and is used as the key for storing and retrieving data about it. One way to generate a Resource-ID is to apply a mapping function to another unique name, such as a user name or a service name. The Resource-ID is used by the distributed database algorithm to determine which peer or peers are responsible for storing the data. That peer is the Responsible Peer, called the Root Peer in the literature. A Resource Record is the block of data stored using the distributed database mechanism that includes information relevant to a specific resource.

The Overlay Name is a human-friendly name identifying a specific overlay, in the format of a portion of a URI, which may or may not have a related record in the DNS. A User Name is a human-friendly name for a user that must be unique within the overlay, and a Service is a capability contributed by a peer to the overlay or to its members, with a unique human-friendly Service Name. The Node-ID is information that uniquely identifies each node within a given overlay; it is not human-friendly, and in a DHT approach it is a numeric value in the hash space, completely independent of the identifier of any user.

The Peer Protocol is the protocol spoken between peers to share information and organize the overlay, implemented using RELOAD. The Client Protocol is the protocol spoken between clients and peers, syntactically the same protocol, the only difference being that clients do not route messages and have not inserted themselves into the overlay. A Peer Protocol Connection is the TLS, DTLS, TCP, UDP or other transport-layer connection over which the RELOAD peer protocol messages are transported. Neighbors are the peers that a peer or client knows of directly and can reach without further lookups.
sections.plainLanguage: Several words matter here. A peer is a member that stores data and forwards messages. A client uses the network without joining it. A resource record is the stored information about a user or a service, and the resource ID is the key it is filed under. The peer that holds a particular record is its responsible peer.

sections.title: How a Call Is Set Up
sections.content:
The overlay functions as a distributed database. A piece of information, a Resource Record, is stored by and retrieved from the database using a key associated with it, the Resource-ID. Each resource must have a unique Resource-ID, and the Resource-ID is also used by the distributed database algorithm to determine the peer or peers that store the record. Information stored in the record of a user can include the full name of the user and the location of the user agents the user is using. Before information about a user can be stored, the user needs a User Name; in RELOAD users are issued certificates, which in the case of centrally signed certificates identify the User Name as well as a number of Resource-IDs where the user may store their information.

Services are located in the same way. A service has a human-friendly Service Name that uniquely identifies it, and the Resource-ID is derived from that name using a function defined by the distributed database algorithm used by the overlay. The RELOAD protocol is extensible and allows many different distributed hash tables to be implemented, but specifies a mandatory-to-implement DHT in the form of a modified Chord DHT.

The basic mechanism works like this. Contact information for a user is stored in the resource record for that user. Assume a user is using a device, called Peer A, that serves as the contact point for the user. The user adds contact information to this resource record, as authorized by the RELOAD certificate mechanism, and the record itself is stored with Peer Z, chosen by the distributed database algorithm in use by the overlay. When the SIP entity coupled with Peer B has an INVITE message addressed to this user, it retrieves the resource record from Peer Z, extracts the contact information for the peers that are contact points for the user, including Peer A, and uses the overlay to establish a connection to Peer A, including any appropriate NAT traversal.

RELOAD is used only to establish the connection. Once the connection is established, messages between the peers are sent using ordinary SIP. The messages between Peers A, B and Z may actually travel through intermediate peers as part of the distributed lookup process, or so as to traverse intervening NATs.
sections.plainLanguage: A user's phonebook entry is filed under a key, and the overlay decides which peer holds it. When a call comes in, the peer handling the call fetches that entry, learns which peer the caller can be reached at, and opens a connection to it. After that the call runs as ordinary SIP, and the overlay steps out of the way.

sections.title: Joining an Overlay and Crossing NATs
sections.content:
Before a peer can attempt to join an overlay, it must first obtain a Node-ID, configuration information, and optionally a set of credentials. The working group does not impose a particular mechanism for how the Peer-ID and credentials are obtained, but the RELOAD protocol specifies the format of the configuration information and how it may be obtained, along with credentials and a Node-ID, from an offline enrollment server.

Once the configuration information is obtained, RELOAD specifies a mechanism whereby a peer may obtain a multicast bootstrap address in the configuration file and broadcast to it to try to locate a bootstrap peer. The peer may also store previous peers it has seen and try those as bootstrap peers, or obtain a bootstrap peer address by some other mechanism. The job of the bootstrap peer is simple: refer the joining peer to a peer, the admitting peer, that will help it join the network. The choice of admitting peer will often depend on the joining peer, for example it may be a peer that will become a neighbor of the joining peer in the overlay, and it is possible that the bootstrap peer also serves as the admitting peer. The admitting peer helps the joining peer learn about other peers and establish connections to them, and during the process the joining peer may be asked to present its credentials, and the peers it contacts may be asked to present theirs.

NAT traversal in P2PSIP using RELOAD treats all peers as equal and establishes a partial mesh of connections between them. Messages from one peer to another are routed along the edges of that mesh until they reach their destination. To make the routing efficient and to avoid the use of standard Internet routing protocols, the partial mesh is organized in a structured manner. If the structure is based on one of the common DHT algorithms, then the maximum number of hops between any two peers is log N, where N is the number of peers in the overlay. Existing connections, along with the Interactive Connectivity Establishment techniques, are used to establish new connections between peers and to allow applications running on peers to connect to one another.
sections.plainLanguage: Joining the network takes three steps. The new peer gets its identifier and configuration, finds a peer already in the network, and that peer introduces it to another peer that helps it settle in. Messages between peers travel along a partial mesh, and because the mesh is ordered by the hash table, a message crosses at most log N hops.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document says it is an overview of existing specifications and introduces no security considerations of its own. Readers are referred to the security considerations of the respective specifications, particularly the RELOAD protocol specification, for further details.

Security is not absent from the picture the document paints. Credentials are part of joining: a joining peer may need to present credentials to prove it has sufficient authority to join the overlay, and the peers it contacts may be asked to present credentials so that the joining peer can verify it is really joining the overlay it wants to. Users are issued certificates in RELOAD, and the certificate mechanism is what authorizes a user to add contact information to their own resource record.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no rules of its own and points to the RELOAD specification for those. Security does appear in the model: a joining peer shows credentials, and a user's certificate is what lets it update its own contact details.

items.title: Peer
items.text: A node in the overlay that provides storage and transport services, with a unique Peer-ID.

items.title: Client
items.text: A node that uses the overlay's services without joining it, storing nothing and forwarding nothing.

items.title: Resource Record
items.text: The block of data held about a resource, keyed by its Resource-ID.

items.title: Responsible Peer
items.text: The peer that stores the resource record for a resource, also called the Root Peer.

items.title: Bootstrap Peer
items.text: The first point of contact for a joining peer, which picks the admitting peer.

items.title: Admitting Peer
items.text: The peer that helps the joining peer join the overlay and meet its neighbours.
